chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, all from Ibn Mahbub from al-Abbas ibn al-Walid from al-Walid ibn Sabih from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who married a free woman and found that she had concealed her status as a slave from him: He said, 'If the one who married her to him was not from her masters, then the marriage is invalid.' I asked, 'What should he do with the dowry that she took from him?' He said, 'If he finds something from what he gave her, let him take it; and if he finds nothing, he has nothing against her.' And if the one who married her to him was her guardian, he shall reclaim from her guardian what she took from him, and for her masters against him is one-tenth of the value of her price if she was a virgin, and if she was not a virgin, half of one-tenth of her value, for what he made lawful of her private part. He said, 'And she observes from him the waiting period of a slave.' I asked, 'If she brings forth a child?' He said, 'Her children from him are free, if the marriage was without the permission of the masters.' This report admits of several interpretations: the first is that this is a denial and astonishment, not a pure report regarding their being free, as if he said, 'How can they be free when the marriage was without the permission of the masters?' And the second is that the one who married her had two witnesses testify before him that she was free, and then her children would be free, which indicates that.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a marriage where the wife conceals her slave status?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfabar outlines the fiqh of 'tadlis' (concealment of status) in marriage, detailing how the validity of the union and financial compensations (mahr and ghurrah) depend on whether the husband knew the woman was a slave and whether her master consented. It further clarifies the status of offspring as free and specifies the waiting period (iddah) as that of a slave, while noting scholarly debate on whether the 'free status' of children is absolute or conditional upon the husband's prior knowledge. This reflects the Shia juristic emphasis on the master's property rights over the slave's marriage contract.
